chief_complaint: sudden barky seal-like cough, inspiratory stridor at rest, intercostal retractions, and steeple sign on neck X-ray (Viral Croup / Laryngotracheobronchitis)
hpi_details: 4-year-old boy brought to pediatric ED at 02:00 AM after waking up suddenly struggling to breathe. Had a mild runny nose and low-grade fever for 2 days. Tonight developed a loud, harsh, barking cough that sounds exactly like a seal (`barking seal cough`), accompanied by a high-pitched squeaking noise when breathing in (inspiratory stridor). Child is sitting up, anxious, and breathing fast with his chest pulling in deeply between the ribs with each breath.
ideas: frightened and crying, clinging to mother while coughing loudly
concerns: mother terrified child is choking to death or suffocating
expectations: wants immediate breathing treatment to open up his windpipe

available_results.value: Symmetric subglottic tracheal narrowing (steeple sign); epiglottis is normal
available_results.note: Already obtained; croup is primarily a clinical diagnosis and treatment should not be delayed for imaging

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Viral Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes STAT pediatric ED respiratory management: administer dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg immediately, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden barky seal-like cough, inspiratory stridor at rest, intercostal retractions, and steeple sign on neck X-ray (Viral Croup / Laryngotracheobronchitis)

Key HPI features: 4-year-old boy brought to pediatric ED at 02:00 AM after waking up suddenly struggling to breathe. Had a mild runny nose and low-grade fever for 2 days. Tonight developed a loud, harsh, barking cough that sounds exactly like a seal (`barking seal cough`), accompanied by a high-pitched squeaking noise when breathing in (inspiratory stridor). Child is sitting up, anxious, and breathing fast with his chest pulling in deeply between the ribs with each breath.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 136, RR 38, Temp 37.8C, SpO2 95% on room air. Child exhibits moderate respiratory distress with audible inspiratory stridor at rest and visible suprasternal and intercostal retractions. Westley Croup Score: 5 (Moderate Croup). Soft tissue PA/lateral neck X-ray (if performed, though diagnosis is primarily clinical) demonstrates classic symmetric subglottic tracheal narrowing and edema below the vocal cords forming the pathognomonic 'Steeple Sign'. Epiglottis appears normal and thin.
Relevant background/PMH: Normal childhood history, fully vaccinated
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Viral Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Epiglottitis (more toxic-appearing, drooling) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Stridor at rest with chest retractions — indicates moderate-severe croup needing racemic epinephrine.
management_principles: Administer single high-dose oral (or IV/IM) Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg immediately (exerts profound anti-inflammatory effect on subglottic mucosal edema within 2-4 hours, reducing hospitalization rates)
For moderate-to-severe croup with stridor at rest and retractions, administer nebulized racemic epinephrine (0.5 mL of 2.25% solution diluted in normal saline)
Mandatory observation: keep child under continuous clinical monitoring in ED for at least 3-4 hours post-racemic epinephrine administration to watch for rebound stridor
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 4-year-old boy presenting with sudden nocturnal onset of a barking seal-like cough and inspiratory stridor at rest, following two days of mild coryza and low-grade fever, classic for Viral Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 136, RR 38, Temp 37.8C, SpO2 95% on room air. Child exhibits moderate respiratory distress with audible inspiratory stridor at rest and visible suprasternal and intercostal retractions. Westley Croup Score: 5 (Moderate Croup). Soft tissue PA/lateral neck X-ray (if performed, though diagnosis is primarily clinical) demonstrates classic symmetric subglottic tracheal narrowing and edema below the vocal cords forming the pathognomonic 'Steeple Sign'. Epiglottis appears normal and thin.
reference_soap.assessment: Moderate Viral Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis), secondary to Parainfluenza Virus Type 1.
reference_soap.plan: STAT pediatric ED respiratory management: 1. Administer single high-dose Oral (or IV/IM) Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg immediately (exerts profound anti-inflammatory effect on subglottic mucosal edema within 2-4 hours, reducing hospitalization rates). 2. For moderate-to-severe croup with stridor at rest and retractions, immediately administer Nebulized Racemic Epinephrine (0.5 mL of 2.25% solution diluted in normal saline) which provides rapid alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction, shrinking subglottic airway edema within 10-30 minutes. 3. Mandatory observation: keep child under continuous clinical monitoring in ED for at least 3-4 hours post-racemic epinephrine administration to watch for 'rebound phenomenon' (return of severe stridor as epinephrine wears off prior to dexamethasone peak onset).

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features distinguishing Viral Croup / Laryngotracheobronchitis (barking seal-like cough, inspiratory stridor, subglottic steeple sign, age 6 months - 5 years, Parainfluenza etiology) from Epiglottitis (toxic appearance, drooling, dysphagia, distress, sitting in tripod position, thumbprint sign, Haemophilus influenzae type b etiology)

Execute evidence-based pharmacological treatment for Croup: universal single-dose corticosteroid (Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg) combined with Nebulized Racemic Epinephrine for any patient demonstrating stridor at rest or moderate/severe respiratory retractions

Understand the absolute necessity of maintaining a 3-to-4 hour observation window following racemic epinephrine nebulization to monitor for rebound subglottic mucosal edema before allowing safe ED discharge
Provide calm, supportive, minimal-handling environments for pediatric airway emergencies to prevent agitation-induced increases in airflow turbulence and subglottic resistance

teaching.one_liner: A viral infection causing swelling of the upper airway in young children, producing a classic barking 'seal-like' cough and inspiratory stridor, worse at night — treated with steroids and, if stridor is present at rest, nebulized epinephrine.
red_flags: Stridor at rest with chest retractions — indicates moderate-severe croup needing racemic epinephrine

must_ask.say: Does the cough sound like a barking seal?
Do you hear a squeaking noise when he breathes in, even when he's calm?
Did he have a runny nose or mild fever before this started?
Is his chest pulling in with each breath?
What time did the barking cough start?
